note: The hour before dawn, the coldest of the night, when the last of the day's warmth is gone. Medieval belief held that dreams dreamed at this hour were true. Dante's three nights on the mountain each end with one: see Cantos 9 and 27.
The outermost planet then known, thought to be cold and to chill the earth when it stood above the horizon.

Geomancers told fortunes from patterns of dots marked at random. One pattern, called Fortuna Major, matched a group of stars in Aquarius and Pisces. Those constellations rise just ahead of Aries, where the sun now is, so dawn is close.

As Virgil explains later in the canto, she stands for the excessive love of worldly goods, purged on the three terraces still to come: avarice, gluttony and lust. Seen plainly, such things are ugly and crippled.

quote: my gaze made her tongue flow freely
note: The lesson of Canto 18 turned into a picture. The worldly good has no beauty of its own. The desire of the one who looks at it lends it color, voice and charm.
In Greek myth the Sirens sang so sweetly that passing sailors steered onto the rocks. They became an image of any pleasure that draws people to ruin.

context: In Homer, Ulysses hears the Sirens tied to his mast and sails safely past. Dante could not read Homer and knew the story only at second hand. He may be confusing the Sirens with the enchantress Circe, or the Siren may simply be lying.

note: Dante does not name her. She has been read as reason, as grace, as Saint Lucy, who carried him up the mountain as he slept in Canto 9, and as Beatrice. Whoever she is, she is the help that wakes the mind from temptation.

context: Dante's reason has been dozing while the Siren sang. The Lady calls it back to its duty.

note: Virgil, on the usual reading, though Dante's Italian does not make clear who does this, and some take it to be the Lady. Called by her, and with his eyes on her, he strips the Siren. Reason, guided from above, shows the false pleasure for what it is.
The truth under the song. The rot was there all along, hidden by the charm that Dante's own desire had given her.

context: It is the morning of Easter Tuesday, Dante's third day on the mountain. The poets circle westward, so the rising sun is behind them.

quote: half an arch of a bridge
note: Bent forward under the weight of his thoughts, his body curved like one side of a bridge.
The angel of the fourth terrace, the angel of zeal. The fanning of his wings removes the fourth letter P, the mark of sloth, from Dante's forehead.

"Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted" (Matthew 5:4), another of the Beatitudes. Why this one suits the slothful is debated. Perhaps they are praised for grieving over their sin instead of shrinking from the effort.

The Siren of the dream. Virgil has seen Dante's dream, as he often reads Dante's thoughts. "Above us" means the three upper terraces, where souls weep for having loved wealth, food and bodily pleasure too much.

quote: strike the earth with your heels
note: Stop brooding and walk. It also means to spurn the earth and its goods.
An image from falconry. The falconer whirls a lure on a cord to call his bird back. God is the falconer, and the wheeling heavens are his lure, calling the eyes of the soul upward.
The terrace of avarice, the greedy love of wealth. Canto 22 adds that the opposite fault, reckless spending, is purged here too.

quote: My soul cleaves to the pavement
note: A verse of Psalm 119 (118 in the Latin Bible), which the souls recite in Latin. It goes on: "give me life according to your word."

The soul assumes the two are spirits who don't need to lie here. A soul stops only on the terraces of the sins it committed and passes freely through the others. This is usually taken to be what Dante gathers from the hidden sense of the words.

quote: your right hands toward the outside
note: Walk with the open edge of the terrace on your right. The poets always circle the mountain this way, following the course of the sun.

context: The pope who held the highest place on earth lies face down in the dust with everyone else, and tells Dante how little the office satisfied him.
Every pope is counted as successor to Peter, the first bishop of Rome. The soul says the phrase in Latin, the language of the Church and of his office.

note: Two towns on the coast east of Genoa. The river between them is the Lavagna. Adrian's family, the Fieschi, were counts of Lavagna.
The papal robe, standing for the office. To keep it out of the mud is to hold the office without disgracing it.

No historical source describes Adrian V as greedy, or records this change of heart. Some scholars think Dante mixed him up with Adrian IV, a pope of the previous century, of whom a similar story about the burden of the papacy was told.

quote: nor could one climb higher in that life
note: He had reached the top of the world and was still not content. Only then did he see that nothing on earth could satisfy him. It is Virgil's teaching in Canto 17: worldly goods cannot make the soul happy.
The life he has now: eternal life.

The penance mirrors the sin. In life they looked only at earthly things, so now their faces are held to the ground. Their hands grasped and their feet chased after gain, so now hands and feet are bound.

quote: I had fallen to my knees
note: Dante kneels out of respect for the papal office, however he judges the men who held it. In the Italian he also addresses Adrian with the formal "you", which he keeps for a very few people in the poem.
The words of the angel in Revelation when John falls down to worship him: "Do not do it. I am a fellow servant with you" (19:10). Earthly rank ends at death.

Christ's saying that in the resurrection people "neither marry nor are given in marriage" (Matthew 22:30). A pope was called the husband of the Church. Death has ended that marriage, and Adrian is now a plain soul like any other.

quote: I ripen what you have described
note: The fruit of repentance. Dante had greeted him as a spirit whose weeping ripens what the soul needs before it can turn to God.

Alagia Fieschi, the daughter of Adrian's brother. She married Moroello Malaspina, who sheltered Dante in the Lunigiana in 1306. The praise is a thank-you to his hosts. Adrian means that she alone would pray for him.
The Fieschi of Genoa, a powerful family that produced two popes and many cardinals.
